name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q01 - Functional matching of human cellular movement mechanisms

questiontext.text:
Match the types of movements in Column I with their corresponding anatomical examples or functions in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Amoeboid movement (i) Protoplasmic streaming in macrophages and leucocytes
B. Ciliary movement (ii) Removal of inhaled dust particles in the trachea
C. Flagellar movement (iii) Swimming of human spermatozoa
D. Muscular movement (iv) Movement of limbs, jaws, and tongue

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Cellular motility via amoeboid action
Amoeboid movement in the human body is exhibited by specialized defensive cells such as macrophages and leucocytes through protoplasmic streaming and pseudopodial extension aided by microfilaments.

Step 2: Epithelial clearance via ciliary action
Ciliary movement is characteristic of ciliated epithelial linings in tubular internal organs, specifically functioning in the trachea to sweep inhaled dust particles and foreign matter upward away from the lungs.

Step 3: Propulsion via flagellar action
Flagellar motility in humans provides the propulsive force required for the swimming of spermatozoa through the female reproductive tract towards the ovum.

Step 4: Biomechanical action via muscular movement
Muscular movement utilizes the contractile properties of muscle tissue to drive gross mechanical actions such as moving the jaws during mastication, the tongue during deglutition, and the limbs during locomotion.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Synthesizing these biological roles confirms that amoeboid movement aligns with macrophage protoplasmic streaming, ciliary movement aligns with tracheal particle clearance, flagellar movement aligns with sperm propulsion, and muscular movement aligns with limb and jaw displacement. Therefore, the combination linking A-(i), B-(ii), C-(iii), and D-(iv) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q02 - Morphological and regulatory traits of human muscle types

questiontext.text:
Match the muscle types in Column I with their histological and functional descriptions in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Skeletal muscle (i) Striated, branched, and involuntary
B. Visceral muscle (ii) Striated, cylindrical, and voluntary
C. Cardiac muscle (iii) Nonstriated, smooth, and involuntary
D. Mesodermal origin (iv) Embryonic germ layer contributing 40 to 50 percent of adult body weight

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Histology and regulation of skeletal muscle
Skeletal muscles are attached to the skeleton, display distinct cross-striations with alternating dark and light bands under microscopy, and are governed directly by voluntary neural pathways.

Step 2: Histology and regulation of visceral muscle
Visceral (smooth) muscles populate the walls of hollow internal viscera, lack transverse striations, and function involuntarily without direct conscious control.

Step 3: Histology and regulation of cardiac muscle
Cardiac muscle forms the contractile walls of the heart; its cells assemble into a branching network, possess cross-striations, and operate involuntarily.

Step 4: Embryonic derivation of muscle tissue
All muscle tissues originate from the embryonic mesoderm and together constitute approximately 40 to 50 percent of total adult body mass.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Correlating each tissue type confirms that skeletal muscle corresponds to striated cylindrical voluntary fibres, visceral muscle corresponds to nonstriated smooth involuntary fibres, cardiac muscle corresponds to striated branched involuntary myocytes, and mesodermal origin accounts for 40 to 50 percent of adult body mass. Therefore, the combination linking A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(i), and D-(iv) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q03 - Microscopic and connective structures of skeletal muscle

questiontext.text:
Match the anatomical terms of skeletal muscle in Column I with their definitions in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Fascia (i) Functional contractile unit between two successive Z lines
B. Sarcolemma (ii) Storehouse of calcium ions in muscle fibres
C. Sarcoplasmic reticulum (iii) Plasma membrane enclosing the sarcoplasm
D. Sarcomere (iv) Common collagenous connective tissue layer binding muscle bundles

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of fascia
Fascia is the tough sheath of collagenous connective tissue that surrounds and binds multiple muscle fascicles into an anatomical muscle.

Step 2: Identification of sarcolemma
The sarcolemma is the specialized lipid bilayer plasma membrane enclosing the multinucleated sarcoplasm of an individual skeletal muscle fibre.

Step 3: Identification of sarcoplasmic reticulum
The sarcoplasmic reticulum is the modified smooth endoplasmic reticulum of muscle fibres that acts as the primary intracellular reservoir and storehouse for calcium ions.

Step 4: Identification of sarcomere
A sarcomere represents the repeating structural and functional unit of contraction along a myofibril, defined as the segment bounded between two successive Z lines.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Correlating each anatomical structure confirms that fascia corresponds to the collagenous connective tissue layer binding fascicles, sarcolemma corresponds to the plasma membrane enclosing sarcoplasm, sarcoplasmic reticulum corresponds to the calcium storehouse, and sarcomere corresponds to the functional unit between successive Z lines. Therefore, the combination linking A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(ii), and D-(i) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q04 - Sarcomere bands lines and structural zones

questiontext.text:
Match the bands and landmarks of a myofibril in Column I with their features in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. I band (i) Elastic line bisecting the light band and anchoring thin filaments
B. A band (ii) Central region of thick filament unoverlapped by thin filaments at rest
C. Z line (iii) Dark anisotropic band containing thick myosin filaments
D. H zone (iv) Light isotropic band containing thin actin filaments

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Structural basis of the I band
The I band (isotropic band) is the light band of the myofibril that consists exclusively of thin actin filaments.

Step 2: Structural basis of the A band
The A band (anisotropic band) is the dark central band containing the thick myosin filaments, which are partially overlapped at their outer margins by thin filaments.

Step 3: Structural role of the Z line
The Z line is a transverse elastic membrane that bisects the I band centrally, serving as the structural anchor for thin actin filaments.

Step 4: Structural definition of the H zone
The H zone is the lighter central region of the A band where thick filaments are not overlapped by thin filaments during the resting state of the sarcomere.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Evaluating each landmark demonstrates that the I band corresponds to the light band containing thin actin filaments, the A band corresponds to the dark anisotropic band containing thick filaments, the Z line corresponds to the elastic line bisecting the I band, and the H zone corresponds to the central unoverlapped thick filament segment. Therefore, the combination linking A-(iv), B-(iii), C-(i), and D-(ii) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q05 - Subunit composition of actin and myosin contractile proteins

questiontext.text:
Match the contractile and regulatory protein elements in Column I with their specific biochemical traits in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. F-actin (i) Polymer formed from monomeric globular actin subunits
B. Tropomyosin (ii) Two filaments running close to F-actins throughout their length
C. Troponin (iii) Complex protein whose subunit masks myosin binding sites at rest
D. Heavy meromyosin (iv) Globular head with short arm possessing active ATPase enzyme

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Polymeric nature of F-actin
Filamentous actin (F-actin) is a linear polymeric chain synthesized through the head-to-tail polymerization of globular actin (G-actin) monomers.

Step 2: Positioning of tropomyosin filaments
Tropomyosin consists of two fibrous strands that run along the helical grooves of the F-actin polymers over their complete longitudinal span.

Step 3: Masking role of troponin
Troponin is a multi-protein complex positioned at regular intervals along tropomyosin; in a resting muscle, one of its subunits physically conceals the active sites on actin to prevent cross-bridge formation.

Step 4: Catalytic structure of heavy meromyosin
Heavy meromyosin (HMM) encompasses the globular head and neck (cross arm) of each meromyosin monomer, housing the catalytic ATPase machinery and actin-binding sites.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Verifying each biochemical component shows that F-actin is the polymer of G-actin, tropomyosin forms two parallel filaments running along F-actins, troponin masks active myosin sites during rest, and heavy meromyosin comprises the ATPase-active globular head and short arm. Therefore, the combination linking A-(i), B-(ii), C-(iii), and D-(iv) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q06 - Biochemical events of excitation contraction coupling

questiontext.text:
Match the physiological events of muscle contraction in Column I with their biochemical roles in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Acetylcholine release (i) Breaks cross-bridges and allows relaxation when newly bound
B. Calcium ion binding (ii) Generates action potential in the sarcolemma
C. ATP binding to myosin (iii) Removes masking of active myosin-binding sites on actin
D. Lactic acid accumulation (iv) Results from anaerobic glycogen breakdown causing muscle fatigue

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Role of acetylcholine in neuromuscular transmission
Acetylcholine released by motor neurons into the neuromuscular junction binds to receptors on the motor end-plate, initiating a propagating action potential across the sarcolemma.

Step 2: Role of calcium binding in cross-bridge activation
Calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind to troponin C, inducing a structural displacement of tropomyosin that uncovers the active binding sites for myosin on actin filaments.

Step 3: Role of ATP binding in cross-bridge detachment
Binding of a fresh ATP molecule to the nucleotide site on the myosin head triggers dissociation of the actomyosin cross-bridge, resetting the cycle.

Step 4: Metabolic origin of muscle fatigue
Sustained, repetitive muscle contraction exceeds aerobic respiratory capacity, driving anaerobic breakdown of glycogen into lactic acid, which accumulates and produces muscular fatigue.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Aligning each event confirms that acetylcholine release triggers sarcolemmal action potentials, calcium binding unmasks actin active sites, ATP binding breaks cross-bridges, and lactic acid accumulation causes fatigue from anaerobic glycogenolysis. Therefore, the combination linking A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(i), and D-(iv) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q07 - Comparative physiological traits of red and white muscle fibres

questiontext.text:
Match the muscle fibre types and pigments in Column I with their metabolic traits in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Red muscle fibres (i) High sarcoplasmic reticulum content and reliance on anaerobic glycolysis
B. White muscle fibres (ii) Red-coloured oxygen-storing pigment giving reddish appearance
C. Myoglobin (iii) Abundant in aerobic muscles for oxidative ATP production
D. Mitochondria (iv) High myoglobin content, plenty of mitochondria, aerobic muscles

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Bioenergetics of red muscle fibres
Red muscle fibres contain elevated levels of myoglobin and numerous mitochondria, enabling sustained aerobic ATP generation without rapid fatigue.

Step 2: Bioenergetics of white muscle fibres
White muscle fibres have low myoglobin concentrations, fewer mitochondria, and a high amount of sarcoplasmic reticulum, depending on anaerobic glycolysis for fast power production.

Step 3: Identity and function of myoglobin
Myoglobin is the red-coloured, iron-bearing protein localized within muscle sarcoplasm that binds and stores oxygen.

Step 4: Role of mitochondria in muscle fibres
Mitochondria are present in large numbers in red aerobic fibres to utilize stored oxygen for oxidative phosphorylation and ATP synthesis.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Correlating each physiological element confirms that red fibres correspond to aerobic muscles rich in myoglobin and mitochondria, white fibres correspond to anaerobic muscles with high sarcoplasmic reticulum, myoglobin corresponds to the oxygen-storing pigment, and mitochondria correspond to aerobic ATP generation organelles. Therefore, the combination linking A-(iv), B-(i), C-(ii), and D-(iii) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q08 - Anatomical distribution of human axial skeletal components

questiontext.text:
Match the components of the axial skeleton in Column I with their numerical or anatomical descriptions in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Cranial bones (i) 14 skeletal elements forming the anterior part of the skull
B. Facial bones (ii) 8 bones forming the hard protective cranium
C. Vertebrochondral ribs (iii) 8th, 9th, and 10th pairs joining the seventh rib via hyaline cartilage
D. Floating ribs (iv) 11th and 12th pairs not connected ventrally

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Enumeration of cranial bones
The human cranium is composed of 8 bones that fuse together to encase and protect the brain.

Step 2: Enumeration of facial bones
The facial skeleton is formed by 14 bones that configure the front architecture of the human skull.

Step 3: Identification of vertebrochondral ribs
The 8th, 9th, and 10th rib pairs do not attach directly to the sternum; instead, their costal hyaline cartilages fuse with the cartilage of the 7th rib, making them vertebrochondral (false) ribs.

Step 4: Identification of floating ribs
The 11th and 12th rib pairs attach dorsally to thoracic vertebrae but have completely unattached anterior ends, designating them as floating ribs.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Reviewing the anatomical details shows that cranial bones number 8, facial bones number 14, vertebrochondral ribs correspond to pairs 8 to 10 joining the 7th rib cartilage, and floating ribs correspond to pairs 11 and 12 lacking ventral attachment. Therefore, the combination linking A-(ii), B-(i), C-(iii), and D-(iv) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q09 - Skeletal features and cavities of appendicular girdles

questiontext.text:
Match the girdle structures in Column I with their anatomical descriptions in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Glenoid cavity (i) Depression in scapula articulating with the head of the humerus
B. Acromion (ii) Expanded flat process of scapular spine articulating with clavicle
C. Acetabulum (iii) Deep cup-shaped cavity for articulation with the head of the femur
D. Pubic symphysis (iv) Ventral junction of pelvic halves containing fibrous cartilage

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Articular nature of the glenoid cavity
The glenoid cavity is a shallow lateral depression located on the scapula beneath the acromion that articulates with the head of the humerus to establish the shoulder joint.

Step 2: Anatomical nature of the acromion process
The acromion is the flattened, expanded lateral continuation of the elevated spine on the dorsal scapula that provides an articulation surface for the clavicle.

Step 3: Articular nature of the acetabulum
The acetabulum is a cup-shaped socket formed at the convergence and fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis that articulates with the head of the femur to form the hip joint.

Step 4: Anatomical nature of the pubic symphysis
The pubic symphysis is the median cartilaginous joint where the two anterior pubic bones of the pelvic girdle articulate ventrally, cushioned by a fibrocartilaginous disc.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
The anatomical evaluation confirms that the glenoid cavity articulates with the humerus, the acromion process articulates with the clavicle, the acetabulum articulates with the femur, and the pubic symphysis joins the pelvic halves via fibrous cartilage. Therefore, the combination linking A-(i), B-(ii), C-(iii), and D-(iv) represents the correct pairing.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_LOCOMOTION_AND_MOVEMENT_MCQ_Q10 - Clinical pathology of muscular and skeletal disorders

questiontext.text:
Match the musculoskeletal disorders in Column I with their primary clinical causes or features in Column II and select the correct option:

Column I Column II
A. Myasthenia gravis (i) Age-related decrease in bone mass commonly due to reduced estrogen
B. Tetany (ii) Autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction
C. Osteoporosis (iii) Rapid spasms in muscle due to low calcium in body fluid
D. Gout (iv) Inflammation of joints caused by accumulation of uric acid crystals

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Clinical profile of Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune pathology in which autoantibodies attack neuromuscular junction receptors, impairing synaptic transmission and resulting in muscle weakness, fatigue, and paralysis.

Step 2: Clinical profile of Tetany
Tetany is characterized by violent spasms and sustained muscle twitches driven by hypocalcemia, an abnormally low concentration of ionized calcium in extracellular body fluids.

Step 3: Clinical profile of Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is an age-related systemic skeletal disorder in which bone mineral density declines and microarchitecture deteriorates, frequently triggered by diminished estrogen levels in postmenopausal individuals.

Step 4: Clinical profile of Gout
Gout is a metabolic inflammatory arthropathy characterized by acute joint inflammation triggered by the deposition and crystallization of uric acid in synovial compartments.

Step 5: Check and Final Conclusion
Comparing all four medical conditions verifies that myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder targeting the neuromuscular junction, tetany stems from low calcium causing muscle spasms, osteoporosis is an age-related loss of bone mass linked to estrogen deficiency, and gout is joint inflammation from uric acid crystals. Therefore, the combination linking A-(ii), B-(iii), C-(i), and D-(iv) represents the correct pairing.
